title: A basket on the Nile (Exodus 2:1–10)
hook: Yocheved hides her baby, Miriam watches, Pharaoh's daughter draws him out

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shiphrah: two midwives quietly refused to kill the baby boys. Your line was the midwives said no. Pharaoh's next order goes to everyone: throw every Hebrew boy into the river. Day seventy-nine.

If you've ever had a newborn in the house, you know: they're not quiet. They cry at three in the morning. They cry when you're trying to be invisible. Now imagine you have to hide one, in a country where soldiers are looking for baby boys. A woman from the tribe of Levi gives birth to a son. She sees that he's good, the text says, and she hides him for three months. Then she can't anymore. So she makes a decision no parent should ever have to make. Today: a basket, a river, and three women.
screen: `A NEWBORN IS NEVER QUIET.` → `HIDDEN FOR THREE MONTHS.` → `THEN SHE CAN'T ANYMORE.`

segments.voice: She takes an ark of bulrushes, waterproofs it with pitch, puts the baby inside, and sets it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile. The Hebrew word for this little basket is tevah. It's the same word used for Noah's ark, and nowhere else in the Torah. Once, a box on the water saved all of life. Now a box on the water carries one baby. Then the text gives us a small, enormous detail: "And his sister stood afar off, to know what would be done to him." She's not named here, but later we learn: Miriam. A young girl, hiding in the reeds, watching. Then Pharaoh's own daughter comes down to bathe. She sees the basket, opens it, and the baby is crying. And she has compassion on him. She knows exactly what this is: one of the Hebrews' children. The daughter of the man who ordered the boys drowned decides to save one. And now Miriam moves. She steps out of the reeds and asks, shall I go and find you a Hebrew woman to nurse the baby for you? Go, says the princess. And Miriam runs and brings the baby's own mother. The mother, the text later tells us, is Yocheved, and now she's being paid to nurse her own son. When he's older, she brings him back to the palace, and Pharaoh's daughter names him Moshe, Moses, saying: "Because I drew him out of the water." Three women. A mother who let go, a sister who watched, and a princess who broke her father's law. The rabbis give that princess a name: Bityah, daughter of God.
screen: `TEVAH: THE SAME WORD AS NOAH'S ARK.` · `HIS SISTER STOOD AFAR OFF.` · `PHARAOH'S DAUGHTER HAS COMPASSION.` · `HIS MOTHER, PAID TO NURSE HIM.` · then, large: `I DREW HIM OUT OF THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch over someone from a distance. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you can't protect directly right now. A grown child who's on their own. A friend going through something they have to face themselves. A parent far away. You can't carry them. But you can watch. Hold them in mind, the way Miriam stood in the reeds. If you pray, you can pray for them. Then think of one small way to let them know someone's watching. The bell holds the time.
Tevah, Hebrew for an ark, a box, the same word used for Noah's ark and nowhere else. A mother lets go, a sister watches, and Pharaoh's daughter draws the baby out and names him Moses.
Your line: someone watches the basket. Today, send one short message to someone you're watching over from far away. Day seventy-nine.

screen: `DAY 79 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MOSES GOES OUT AND SEES.`

howItsDone: Jewish tradition honors the women of the Exodus story, Yocheved, Miriam, the midwives and Pharaoh's daughter, whom the rabbis call Bityah, and teaches that Israel was redeemed from Egypt in the merit of righteous women.

original.note: Hebrew: an ark, a box. used only for Noah's ark and Moses' basket.

trapdoor: what you thought: a baby in a basket floating down the river.
what it means: three women risking everything: a mother who let go, a sister who watched, and a princess who broke her father's law.
what a scholar hears: tevah appears only in Genesis 6–9 and Exodus 2. Moshe is explained by mashah, to draw out. the name Bityah comes from 1 Chronicles 4:18 and the midrash.

Bityah: 1 Chronicles 4:18 names 'Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh'; Leviticus Rabbah 1:3 explains the name as 'daughter of God'. Confirm citation.
